facts.claim: "Make It Rain" is the closing track (track 10, 4:51) on Foy Vance's album From Muscle Shoals, released 28 June 2019 on Gingerbread Man Records.
From Muscle Shoals was co-produced by Vance with Ben Tanner and recorded at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama.
Two of the original Muscle Shoals 'Swampers' rhythm section, Spooner Oldham (keys) and David Hood (bass), played on the album.
The album was recorded completely live with all the players in the room. Vance said the first song cut, "You Get To Me", set the precedent for the whole record.
"Make It Rain" is one of two tracks on From Muscle Shoals (with "Be with Me") that are punched-up versions of earlier works. The song had already been in circulation years before 2019.

Ed Sheeran covered "Make It Rain" for the 2 December 2014 'Red Rose' episode of Sons of Anarchy. Sheeran asked to cover it because the song opens with the line 'the sins of my father', which the show's creator had requested.

Vance found old demos labelled 'Soul' and 'Americana'. The 'Soul' songs became the basis of From Muscle Shoals, and the 'Americana' songs became To Memphis, recorded at Sam Phillips Recording Studio in Memphis.
Vance was born in Bangor, Northern Ireland, in 1974. His preacher father moved the family to Oklahoma, and the family returned to Northern Ireland, settling in Belfast, by the time he was five.
Vance signed to Ed Sheeran's Gingerbread Man Records in November 2015 and released The Wild Swan on 13 May 2016. From Muscle Shoals followed on 28 June 2019 and To Memphis on 6 September 2019.

research.lineage: The album pays homage to the southern soul and Americana traditions of Muscle Shoals and Memphis, recorded at FAME Studios with players from the original Muscle Shoals rhythm section.

draft:
"Even so, Lord just the same." That's the line that holds **Make It Rain** together, and it's a strange thing to pray. Foy Vance has just admitted the fire will hurt. He knows the tears might be wasted. He asks for it anyway, eight times over in every chorus, as if saying it enough could turn dread into consent.

The song opens with inherited weight: "When the sins of my father weigh down in my soul," followed at once by a mother's pain that "will not let me go." Nothing gets confessed in detail. The narrator doesn't say what was done or by whom. What's left is the feeling of carrying something you didn't choose and can't put down. The fire from the sky is meant to "refine the purest of kings," so the suffering is supposed to purify. But the second verse loses that confidence. The ground keeps getting harder, the hunger more profound, and the tears "may as well be in vain." Surrender and something close to despair sit right next to each other, and the song never settles which one wins.

Then the third verse turns outward. The sea stops at the shore, "just like the riches of grandeur never reach the poor." A private plea for cleansing becomes a demand for justice, with lightning as veins and thunder as applause, "when it's time to make a change." The refrain that follows runs twice as long as before. The prayer gets louder because now it's for everybody.

The playing gives that prayer room to breathe. It's a slow, bluesy shuffle. An acoustic guitar strums the chords, the bass walks underneath, and the drums keep a simple beat. The room is warm and medium-sized, with natural reverb and a slightly raw edge. Vance sings in a raspy, soulful voice and holds his notes long, so each "make it rain" lands with weight instead of urgency.

That rawness fits the record it closes. Vance cut *From Muscle Shoals* at FAME Studios with co-producer Ben Tanner. It was recorded live with all the players in the room, and Swampers Spooner Oldham and David Hood are on the album. The song itself is older. It's one of two tracks reworked for the record, and it had already reached a wide audience in 2014, when Ed Sheeran covered it for *Sons of Anarchy*. He chose it because the show's creator wanted a song about the sins of a father. Here it returns to the southern soul tradition its gospel phrasing was always reaching for.

It sticks because it lets you ask for the hard thing out loud, knowing it will hurt and wanting it anyway.
